lines.say: For as long as anyone alive can remember, Germany has had more people than Britain. Today, 84 million against 70.

lines.note: UN projection: the UK passes Germany in 2059
lines.say: But on the United Nations' central projection, the UK passes Germany in 2059. Italy has already started shrinking. And Poland could lose half its people by 2100.
Here are Europe's biggest populations over 150 years, from 1950 to 2100.

card: UN figures up to 2023. After that, the UN's middle scenario. Source: UN World Population Prospects 2024
lines.say: First, what you're looking at. Up to 2023, these are the United Nations' estimates. After that, they're projections: the UN's middle scenario, based on assumptions about births, deaths and migration.

card: They show where today's trends lead. Projected years have striped bars
lines.say: Projections aren't predictions. They show where today's trends lead if they carry on. Whenever the chart is showing projected years, the bars are striped.

card: Russia as the whole country. Turkey, mostly in Asia, is left out: it would be second
lines.say: Russia is shown as the whole country, including the part in Asia. We've left out Turkey, which lies mostly in Asia. With 88 million people, it would be second. And Germany is shown within today's borders, east and west together, for every year.
1950. Russia has 103 million people. Germany, 70 million. The UK, 50.
Italy, 46. France, 42. Ukraine, 37. Spain has 28 million, and Poland 25.
Then comes the baby boom, and decades of growth almost everywhere. Russia peaks at the start of the nineties, at almost 150 million, and Ukraine soon after, at 52.
2000. Russia is already shrinking, at 147 million. Germany has 82. France and the UK, 59 each. Italy, 57.
Ukraine is down to 50 million.
Over the next quarter of a century, the countries in Western Europe keep growing slowly. Most of those further east keep shrinking.
2025. Russia, 144 million. Germany, 84. The UK, just under 70. France, 67.
Italy, 59. Spain, 48. Ukraine, 39. And Poland, 38.
Here are six of them as lines. Look at Italy. Its population peaked in 2014, at 60.7 million. Since then, it has lost about one and a half million people.

lines.note: Spain, Poland and Germany: at or near their peak
lines.say: Spain, Poland and Germany are at, or very close to, their highest ever. On the UN's numbers, all three start falling from here.
Now we're in projection territory. Everything from here on is the UN's middle scenario: where today's births, deaths and migration lead if they carry on.
By 2050, Germany is down to 78 million, and the UK is up to 75 and a half.
France has 68 million. Italy has lost more than 7 million people, and is down to 52.

lines.note: 2059 · the UK passes Germany, at 76 million
lines.say: And in 2059, the lines cross. With about 76 million each, the UK passes Germany.

By 2100, the UK has 74 million people, and Germany 71. The UK itself peaks in the early 2070s, then starts to shrink as well. France is the only one here still growing almost to the end of the century, to 68 and a half million in the 2090s.
Italy has fallen to 35 million. Spain, to 33. And Poland, to 19 million: half of what it has today.
Here's the full ranking for 2100. Russia is still first, at 126 million, almost 18 million fewer than today. Then the UK, Germany and France, and then a long drop.
Ukraine falls to 15 million, fewer than the Netherlands. Romania, which peaked in 1991 at 23 million, is down to 11.
So why do the lines bend? Two forces decide most of it. The first is births. Without migration, a country needs about 2.1 children per woman to keep its population steady.
No big European country is close. In 2023, France had the most, at 1.6. The UK, 1.6 too. Germany, 1.4. Poland, 1.3. Italy and Spain, 1.2. And Ukraine, fewer than one.
Fewer births means that in many countries, more people now die each year than are born.
In 2023, Germany had almost 4 more deaths than births for every 1,000 people. Italy, almost 5. Ukraine, 7 and a half. The UK and France still had slightly more births than deaths.
The second force is migration. And here's a surprise: Germany has more immigrants than the UK. One in five people living in Germany was born abroad. In the UK, about one in six.
Migration is what has kept Germany growing. But as its population ages, the gap between deaths and births gets wider, and on the UN's numbers, migration no longer makes up for it.
Spain has almost as high a share of immigrants as Germany, but one of Europe's lowest birth rates. Poland has very few immigrants, and many young Poles live and work abroad.
Behind all of this is age. The median age is the age that splits a country in half: half the people are older, half younger. In 1950, it was 27 and a half in Italy. Today, it's 48.
Germany's median age is 45. The UK's is 40, which is one reason Britain keeps growing for longer. And Poland's has jumped from 25 to 42. On the UN's numbers, it reaches 52 by 2050.
For Ukraine, the war since 2022 and millions of refugees have changed the numbers sharply. Its long-term projection is especially uncertain.

take: In 2059, on the UN's central projection
lines.say: Three things to take away. One: on the UN's central projection, the UK passes Germany in 2059, because Germany has more deaths than births.

take: Italy, Spain and Poland lose a third or more
lines.say: Two: Italy, Spain and Poland are at or past their peak. By 2100, each could lose a third or more of its people.

take: Every country here will have more older people to support
lines.say: Three: a smaller population isn't a disaster by itself. But fewer young people supporting more older people is a challenge every country on this chart will face.
